bottlenecks.description: High-dimensional heterogeneous data integration: omics layers have incompatible scales, distributions, and feature spaces (e.g., sparse mutation data vs dense expression profiles), making joint modeling statistically and computationally challenging
bottlenecks.evidence: Baião et al. 2025, Brief Bioinform 26(4):bbaf355, doi:10.1093/bib/bbaf355; Sibilio et al. 2025, doi:10.1093/bioadv/vbag108

bottlenecks.description: Batch effects across omics layers: non-biological technical variation from different platforms, protocols, and processing batches confounds biological signals and compromises reproducibility
bottlenecks.evidence: Sibilio et al. 2025, doi:10.1093/bioadv/vbag108; Hemme 2025, PMC12937625

bottlenecks.description: Missing data and incomplete multi-view observations: integrated samples commonly have one or more entirely missing omics layers with various missing patterns, reducing effective sample sizes
bottlenecks.evidence: Lee et al. 2021, PMLR v130, 'A Variational Information Bottleneck Approach to Multi-Omics Data Integration'; Baião et al. 2025, doi:10.1093/bib/bbaf355

bottlenecks.description: Quadratic memory and runtime scaling: many multimodal integration methods (e.g., MMD-MA, MOFA+) scale as O(n²) in the number of cells, becoming prohibitive beyond tens of thousands of samples
Curse of dimensionality with small sample sizes: omics studies typically have n<
bottlenecks.evidence: PMC7281435, 'Metabolomics and Multi-Omics Integration: A Survey'; FLASH, npj Syst Biol Appl 2025, doi:10.1038/s41540-025-00614-x

bottlenecks.description: I/O and data transfer bottlenecks: loading multi-terabyte datasets (VCF ~5TB for 10k samples, scRNA-seq ~2TB for 100k cells) exceeds typical node memory; CPU-GPU transfer limits scaling
bottlenecks.evidence: PMC6823959, 'Scaling computational genomics to millions of individuals with GPUs'; Broad Institute talk 2025, 'Infrastructure and modeling challenges in single-cell omics'

bottlenecks.description: Feature space discrepancy across modalities: different omics layers have distinct feature spaces (genes vs chromatin regions vs metabolites), requiring complex alignment strategies

np_hard_problems.problem: Optimal feature selection in high-dimensional omics data
np_hard_problems.complexity: NP-hard: search space includes 2^n - 1 feature subsets for n features; no polynomial-time algorithm achieves minimax-optimal recovery under worst-case designs
current_approaches: Filter methods (t-test, ANOVA, Wilcoxon, mutual information, MRMR)
Wrapper methods with metaheuristic optimization (SPHMO, genetic algorithms)
Embedded methods (LASSO, elastic net, tree-based importance)
Hybrid filter-plus-elimination (FLASH, MAFS with multi-head attention)
Quantum-inspired QUBO formulations for gene selection
gaps: No polynomial-time algorithm achieves information-theoretic optimal sample complexity
Heuristic methods yield inconsistent performance across datasets
Statistical-computational trade-off: efficient algorithms require stronger design conditions (restricted eigenvalues, incoherence)
Scalability limited to feature spaces of ~18,000 features in practice

np_hard_problems.problem: Best subset selection for multi-omics biomarker discovery
np_hard_problems.complexity: NP-hard: statistically minimax optimal but computationally intractable; exponential in the number of features
current_approaches: Graphlet screening for sparse Gram matrices
AdaSub / local search with polynomial adaptivity
Two-stage ETS framework with polylog time per estimate
gaps: Efficient algorithms incur additional sample complexity cost inversely proportional to squared restricted eigenvalue
No method simultaneously achieves minimax statistical optimality and polynomial computational complexity
Multi-omics extension of best subset selection remains largely unexplored

np_hard_problems.problem: Network alignment and matching across omics layers
np_hard_problems.complexity: NP-hard: subgraph isomorphism and graph matching problems; exact alignment of multi-layer networks is computationally infeasible at scale
current_approaches: Graph-linked unified embedding (GLUE) with guidance graphs
gaps: Scalable exact alignment remains elusive for atlas-scale datasets
Prior knowledge graphs may be incomplete or biased
Unpaired data integration requires approximate matching with quality guarantees

np_hard_problems.problem: Multi-objective optimization for omics layer selection and integration strategy
np_hard_problems.complexity: NP-hard: selecting optimal omics layers and integration architecture involves combinatorial optimization over 2^k possible layer combinations and multiple competing objectives
current_approaches: Unsupervised factor analysis (MOFA+) for automatic relevance determination
gaps: No principled method for determining which omics layers to include a priori
Integration strategy selection (early/intermediate/late) remains largely heuristic
Trade-offs between interpretability and predictive performance not formally characterized

sota_approaches.name: MOFA+ (Multi-Omics Factor Analysis+)
sota_approaches.description: Bayesian group factor analysis framework for unsupervised integration of multi-modal single-cell data; decomposes variance into shared and view-specific factors; handles missing data natively via probabilistic framework; scales to ~100k cells
sota_approaches.citation: Argelaguet et al. 2020, Genome Biol 21:111, doi:10.1186/s13059-020-02015-1; original MOFA: Argelaguet et al. 2018, Mol Syst Biol 14:e8124, doi:10.15252/msb.20178124

sota_approaches.name: Seurat WNN (Weighted Nearest Neighbor)
sota_approaches.description: Unsupervised framework learning cell-specific modality weights for integrative multimodal analysis; constructs multimodal reference atlases; scales to >1M cells with dictionary learning bridge integration in v5

sota_approaches.name: GLUE (Graph-Linked Unified Embedding)
sota_approaches.description: Deep learning framework using variational graph autoencoders with prior knowledge guidance graphs to link omics-specific feature spaces; achieves sublinear computational scalability; first method to integrate millions of cells accurately

sota_approaches.name: LIGER (Integrative Non-negative Matrix Factorization)
sota_approaches.description: Joint matrix factorization learning shared and dataset-specific metagenes; aligns datasets across platforms and species; scales to ~500k cells

sota_approaches.name: LSMMD-MA (Large-Scale MMD-MA)
sota_approaches.description: Reformulated MMD-MA using primal optimization and KeOps CUDA framework for symbolic matrix computation; scales linearly in memory to 1M cells per modality, two orders of magnitude beyond existing implementations

sota_approaches.name: scVI / totalVI (Variational Autoencoders)
sota_approaches.description: Deep generative models for multi-omics integration; multimodal VAEs with product-of-experts for joint latent space inference; handles imputation, augmentation, and batch effect correction

sota_approaches.name: mixOmics / DIABLO
sota_approaches.description: PLS-based supervised multi-omics integration for biomarker discovery; sparse MB-PLS regression for regulatory module identification; widely used for feature selection
sota_approaches.citation: Rohart et al. 2017, PLoS Comput Biol 13:e1005752, doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1005752

failure_modes.mitigation: Regularization (LASSO, elastic net), cross-validation, dimensionality reduction before integration, Bayesian priors with automatic relevance determination

failure_modes.mode: Batch effect propagation through integration pipeline
failure_modes.mitigation: Harmony batch correction, scMerge2 for cross-study harmonization, anchor-based integration (Seurat), explicit batch covariates in probabilistic models
Cell-specific modality weighting (Seurat WNN), factor-wise variance decomposition (MOFA+), adversarial alignment (GLUE)

failure_modes.mode: Distortion from naive imputation of missing omics data
failure_modes.mitigation: Probabilistic frameworks with native missing data handling (MOFA+, scVI), product-of-experts for incomplete multi-view observations (DeepIMV), avoiding mean imputation

failure_modes.mode: Out-of-distribution generalization failure in cell type annotation
failure_modes.mitigation: Hierarchical cross-entropy loss incorporating cell type ontologies, reference-based mapping with dictionary learning (Seurat v5), domain adaptation techniques

failure_modes.mode: Re-identification of individuals from integrated multi-omics profiles
failure_modes.mitigation: Federated learning with differential privacy, k-anonymity, homomorphic encryption, secure multi-party computation, data residency controls

hardware_requirements.minimum: 32 GB RAM, 8 CPU cores, 500 GB SSD storage; sufficient for bulk multi-omics integration of ~100 samples with ~20k features per modality
hardware_requirements.recommended: 256+ GB RAM, 32+ CPU cores, NVIDIA A100 40GB+ GPU, 10+ TB NVMe storage; required for single-cell multi-omics integration at 100k+ cell scale and deep learning model training

regulations: GDPR (EU): strict consent requirements, right to be forgotten, cross-border transfer restrictions, special category data classification for genomic data
HIPAA (US): protected health information safeguards, access controls, audit trails, breach notification requirements
European Health Data Space (EHDS): emerging framework for cross-border health data sharing
FAIR principles: Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable data management
ISO 27001/27701: information security and privacy information management
challenges: Re-identification risk: multi-omics profiles act as 'molecular fingerprints' harder to anonymize than single data types; rare genotype + metabolic profile combinations can uniquely identify individuals
Cross-jurisdictional conflicts: GDPR, HIPAA, PIPL, and regional laws create conflicting requirements for cross-border data sharing
Federated learning governance: differential privacy incurs 15-35% utility loss; blockchain imposes 40-50% computational overhead
Consent management: broad consent for specific research purposes complicates multi-omics data sharing; automated consent tracking across integrated datasets needed
Data residency requirements: keeping data within jurisdictional boundaries while enabling collaborative analysis
Right to be forgotten: purging specific data points across all integrated omics layers is computationally intensive without centralized governance
Model-level privacy: trained ML models can leak training data; adversarial robustness and secure aggregation needed
